title.value: Eyes on Your Typing: Snooping Finger Motions on Virtual Keyboards
Eyes on Your Typing: Snooping Finger Motions on Virtual Keyboards

abstract.value: The rapid growth of augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies has introduced immersive digital experiences for consumers across numerous fields, including banking, education, and professional spheres. In these environments, head-mounted displays (HMDs) enable users to interact with virtual objects through head and hand tracking. In particular, virtual keyboards are emerging as a primary input method, allowing users to type directly with their hands-eliminating the need for additional devices and adding convenience for portable HMD use. However, this direct hand-based typing introduces new security concerns, namely subtle head movements that occur during direct hand-based typing can unintentionally reveal private information. In this paper, we propose SNOOPFINGER, a novel side-channel attack that leverages head movement data, which is accessible without additional user permissions, to estimate typed inputs on a virtual keyboard. Unlike previous methods, SNOOPFINGER uniquely employs a cross-modality approach, relying solely on head movement data to infer hand-typed inputs without the use of controllers. Additionally, our approach is designed to identify a victim's typed inputs without requiring prior access to extensive head movement data from the victim or other users. In an experiment involving 24 participants, SNOOPFIN-GER achieved high inference accuracy rates, with an average Top-1 accuracy of 55.2% for word inference and 68.8% for sentence reconstruction. Finally, we discuss potential mitigation strategies to counteract such attacks. Our findings reveal critical privacy risks associated with direct hand-based typing in AR/VR environments, demonstrating how zero-permission sensor data can be exploited to obtain private information. 4340 2025 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)

The rapid growth of augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies has introduced immersive digital experiences for consumers across numerous fields, including banking, education, and professional spheres. In these environments, head-mounted displays (HMDs) enable users to interact with virtual objects through head and hand tracking. In particular, virtual keyboards are emerging as a primary input method, allowing users to type directly with their hands-eliminating the need for additional devices and adding convenience for portable HMD use. However, this direct hand-based typing introduces new security concerns, namely subtle head movements that occur during direct hand-based typing can unintentionally reveal private information. In this paper, we propose S NOOP FINGER , a novel side-channel attack that leverages head movement data, which is accessible without additional user permissions, to estimate typed inputs on a virtual keyboard. Unlike previous methods, S NOOP FINGER uniquely employs a cross-modality approach, relying solely on head movement data to infer hand-typed inputs without the use of controllers. Additionally, our approach is designed to identify a victim's typed inputs without requiring prior access to extensive head movement data from the victim or other users. In an experiment involving 24 participants, S NOOP FIN- GER achieved high inference accuracy rates, with an average T op-1 accuracy of 55.2% for word inference and 68.8% for sentence reconstruction. Finally, we discuss potential mitigation strategies to counteract such attacks. Our findings reveal critical privacy risks associated with direct hand-based typing in AR/VR environments, demonstrating how zero-permission sensor data can be exploited to obtain private information. 1. Introduction The rapid development of augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies has significantly trans- formed user interaction in digital environments. According to worldwide market research and consulting organization Precedence Research, the global AR and VR headsets mar- ket size estimate in 2022 was USD 6.78 billion, and that figure is expected to reach about USD 142.5 billion by 2032, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 35.6% during the forecast period from 2023 to 2032 [3]. This indicates increasing integration of the technology into various fields, such as banking [2], [4], tourism [1], educa- tion [9], [17], and professional spheres [5], [6], [10], [16]. Head-mounted displays (HMDs) are central features of these experiences, providing users a fully immersive interface that allows them to engage with virtual content in ways that feel natural and intuitive. These HMDs typically employ sophisticated head and hand tracking technologies that en- able users to seamlessly navigate virtual environments. This functionality is critical for creating a sense of presence and allows users to interact with virtual objects and interfaces as they would in the real world. Among these interfaces, virtual keyboards have emerged as a key input tool, particularly for tasks that require text input. Instead of using a physical keyboard, users can type by pressing virtual keys, which simulates the traditional typing experience in a digital space. In particular, direct hand-based typing on a virtual keyboard is gradually becoming a primary typing method in VR. This approach eliminates the need for additional hardware, such as controllers, providing significant convenience when using portable HMDs. Thanks to these advantages, researchers have been exploring various ways to further develop direct hand-based typing in VR environments. [22], [26], [29], [30], [34] While this direct hand-based typing on virtual keyboards feels intuitive and enhances the user experience and conve- nience, it also introduces previously unexplored security vul- nerabilities. A critical concern arises from the fact that when users type using their fingers on virtual keyboards, their head and eye movements tend to correlate naturally with their hand movements. These movements, although subtle and seemingly benign, could inadvertently leak private in- formation, such as the text that is being typed. This creates an attack vector in the context of AR/VR environments. Accordingly, we focus on the following research question: Can the subtle head movements that occur when a user types on a virtual keyboard with their fingers be used to infer the text being entered? In this paper, we propose a novel side-channel attack that exploits head movement data to infer direct hand- based typing on a virtual keyboard. For this method, we glean the user's typed input through gaze direction derived from head movement data. Importantly, head movement data 4340 DOI 10.1109/SP61157.2025.00227 (e.g., orientation and position) does not require explicit user permissions, making it accessible to malicious background apps. The reason for this unrestricted access is that AR/VR applications must constantly track the user's head pose to update the virtual environment's rendering in real time [50]. As a result, this inherent feature of AR/VR systems makes our attack not only feasible but also difficult to detect. There have been several studies focused on inferring virtual keyboard inputs, but most rely on the same modal- ity (e.g., inferring head-typed inputs from head movement or hand-typed inputs from hand movement). For example, Meteriz et al. demonstrated that hand movement data can be used to estimate the letters typed using hand movements on a virtual keyboard [41]. Similarly, Wu et al. used controller tracking data (which we can also consider hand movement data) to infer typed inputs on virtual keyboards [53]. Luo et al. showed that head movement data can be used to estimate the letters typed via head gaze commit (HGC), for which users aim their head at specific keys to input text [38]. More recently, one study explored a cross-modality tech- nique involving hand-typed inputs being inferred from head movements. Slocum et al. demonstrated that it is possible to gauge typed inputs using head movement data [50], but this study primarily examines typing on a virtual keyboard using controllers rather than direct finger input. Additionally, the inference model requires prior access to extensive training data. In contrast, our approach uniquely focuses on inferring direct hand-based typing-meaning users type directly on a virtual keyboard with their fingers rather than using a controller-and it does not rely on large volumes of training data. In addressing the core research questions, we encoun- tered several key challenges: (1) How can we accurately detect when user typing starts and ends? (2) How can we distinguish between letters typed within a word and those that serve as word delimiters? (3) How can we infer typed inputs based on gaze direction when the virtual keyboard's position varies dynamically? Unlike physical keyboards, virtual keyboards in AR/VR environments are not fixed in position or size. While users can use a controller to type from a distance without repositioning the virtual keyboard at its initial setting, direct hand-based typing typically requires the keyboard to be relocated closer to the user for comfort and accuracy. When the virtual keyboard is too far away, direct hand-based typing becomes more challenging and un- comfortable, as the user must extend their arms, potentially decreasing typing accuracy. Therefore, the direction of the user's gaze toward the virtual keyboard may vary depending on the keyboard's relocated position. Consequently, relying solely on gaze direction estimated from head movements could lead to discrepancies in the inferred input. In this paper, we term our approach S NOOP FINGER , as it focuses on snooping finger -based inputs on virtual keyboards. Our primary contributions are summarized as follows: • To the best of our knowledge, S NOOP FINGER is the first cross-modality attack to infer direct hand- typed inputs on a virtual keyboard within AR/VR systems by leveraging only head movement data that is accessible without explicit user permissions. This underscores the potential for user privacy exposure through attacks based on sensor data. • We propose a methodology to identify user-typed in- puts in virtual 3D space solely from head movement data. By converting head movement data into 3D gaze direction within a virtual environment and then projecting and normalizing it onto a 2D plane, we derive normalized 2D gaze points. Additionally, we introduce the Backward Key Inference Tree (Back- Tree), which allows an adversary to infer a victim's typed inputs within the 3D virtual environment. • Our approach assumes a realistic yet challenging scenario in which the adversary does not have prior access to extensive data about the victim or other users. In other words, our method neither requires the adversary to gather labeled training data to build an inference model nor demands substantial data volumes to effectively initiate the attack. • To evaluate the feasibility of S NOOP FINGER , we develop a malicious background application capable of inconspicuously collecting head movement data. Using this application, we collected head movement data from 24 users while they typed on a virtual key- board with their fingers in an AR/VR system. The results show an average Top-1 accuracy of 55.2% for word inference and 68.8% for sentence reconstruc- tion. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that SNOOP FINGER could be effective with different typ- ing postures (e.g., one-handed, two-handed, sitting, and standing), highlighting the applicability of our approach in real-world usage scenarios. • We discuss potential mitigation strategies to counter such cross-modality attacks and provide insights into improving sensor management policies within AR/VR systems. 2. Related Works 2.1. Key Inference Attacks on AR/VR Systems Motion-based Approach. Motion-based approaches can be categorized as same-modality, cross-modality, or multi- modality. A same-modality approach uses input and out- put actions that originate from the same source of motion (e.g., using hand movements to infer hand-typed inputs or head movements for head-typed inputs). A cross-modality approach leverages one type of motion to predict or infer actions from a different modality (e.g., using head move- ments for hand-typed inputs). A multi-modality approach combines data from multiple sources of motion (e.g., both hand and head movements) to infer actions. 4341
